text_fidelity_a:
Lost Cities - The Board Game You can move your five explorers (you don't need to use them all) on any of five paths. You can move one square forward on each color if you play a card of that color that is higher than the last card you played. So if you play a two, you can play a three or a four etc, to move forward. You can't play a lower card, but you can discard it, and your opponents can pick it up. Along the way you get bonus points and artifacts to raise your score. Three rounds makes a game.

This game is supposed to take 30 minutes to an hour, but I have yet to find even a three player version go that fast. There is too much strategy and planning involved. You need to think about what cards you need now, what you need later, what your opponents might use if you discard a card, and how many "for later" cards you can retain. You need to decide when to bite the bullet and take a big number jump (limiting your later moves) and when to hold off.

It definitely plays better with more than two players. It's fast to learn, and a lot of fun.
text_fidelity_b: Lost Cities - The Board Game

text_fidelity_a:
Friendly Loom 7" Potholder Kit Green Metal Loom and Bright Rainbow Color Cotton Loops, Makes 2 Potholders, MADE IN THE USA by Harrisville Designs. I had almost forgotten about this little loom -- I first learned how to make these potholders in the 1950s even before I started school (I was probably 5 yrs old). My brother and I spent many summers working on these and selling them around the neighborhood to augment our $0.25/week allowance. My mother taught us how to make them and kept us supplied with the loops while we came up with our own designs.

One thing I remember very clearly -- she avoided nylon loops, preferring instead cotton loops. Why? Because the nylon loops could melt at the temperatures commonly encountered when using cast iron pans and metal baking dishes in hot ovens. I retained that memory, so when I saw this kit available with cotton loops, I knew I needed to try it one more time.

The major difference I see is in the length of the "prongs" in the loom -- I recall them being a little longer. Also, the metal weaving hook was a bit longer. But other than that, the design and construction are close to what I used as a child.

The package from Amazon arrived earlier today, and I quickly put together the potholder in the photo. It took probably an hour -- perhaps a bit longer, but not much. There are enough loops for a couple of pot holders and enough colors to mix and match. Follow the directions, especially the part about finishing -- pulling one of the loops on each finished edge back over a loom peg to keep the rest of the loops on the adjacent and opposite sides from popping off the loom. Take your time with this part -- it's easy to want to hurry to finish it, but it can be a bit "fiddly."

Very happy with this -- I've already ordered additional loops in specific colors to coordinate with my kitchen colors so I can make several of these to use as potholders as well as hot pads/trivets.
text_fidelity_b: Friendly Loom 7" Potholder Kit Green Metal Loom and Bright Rainbow Color Cotton Loops, Makes 2 Potholders, MADE IN THE USA by Harrisville Designs.

text_fidelity_a:
Hygge Games How did You Know That? – Trivia Party Game, White As a lover of board games… Our family members each receive a new addition to the game closet in their stocking every year… With kids off to college- I am constantly looking for new and fun options that don’t take a lot explaining or, learning and can peek their interest, liking them to be a bit competitive yet, can be played with minimal effort- So, a hard combo to find! So, I’m happy to say… “How did You know That-“ falls into this category!!

DID YOU KNOW THAT is easy enough to learn and that’s a perk! Also, a big plus is the fact, it’s easy to explain it to those who have a tendency to not pay attention during rule reading (we all know a few of “those type” people- ha ha..!!) BUT, with an easy concept they’ll be playing like pros in no time.. LOVE the fact, this game can be tweaked and adapted if necessary.. and we always love those! (Anything that allows you to simplify or shorten a game as needed.. is like sprinkles on top!)

Basic idea: one person reads 4 questions in a row off of x1 card. All other players write their 4 answers down… THEN, players will correct answers as revealed for all 4 questions asked. giving x1 pt. per correct answer. If only x1 person gets it right the crowd shouts “how did you know that!” and gets double points. Its that simple..

This is full of Quirky odd questions at various levels of some useful/not trivia! Winner is whoever has most points at the end of game..
Best part is: YOU decide do you play to a certain point level (1st one to 10, 20 wins?) OR, do you give everyone certain amount of cards so, everyone has a turn or two to read questions.. if so then, at the end of all reveals.. they tally up those points received to see who’s the winner! That’s it..!!!

This would make a great game for the dorms- (especially during the time of the pandemic.. these kids have a lot of Shelter in place/quarantine time!) for those old enough, I could see it turning this into a drinking game of sorts (good or, bad?!) it would easily adapt.
Definitely, feel this is geared toward older teens or, adults.. it’s too hard for younger kids. I do feel this has a niché for academics and know it alls! Any with mega time spent learning, reading, gaining random facts off the Internet- it’s a great way to share that trivial academia skills.. Ha! Some things will just be fun facts you picked up thru life, in elementary school or, info. From those who’ve raised you.. tossed with real trivia facts. So, the smartest person doesn’t always win!? Fun for a competitive group with a plethora of knowledge and facts to share!!
Played with our college kids over holiday and it went back to the dorm bc, of its fun factor- with x3 college kids and/or, recent graduates.. we had a ball! I hope this info can help your decision.. feel free to let me know!
text_fidelity_b: Hygge Games How did You Know That? – Trivia Party Game, White

The concept is simple in that you need to just try to anticipate what others will play, sort of like rock-paper-scissors. But this game can have multiple players at a time and last until someone either collects enough winning cards (pieces of garbage) or is the last player standing.
The caveats are that you have the ability to "play it safe", which can avoid getting out if someone accuses you of trying to steal on your turn. This can lead to many rounds where nothing happens as someone needs to steal or accuse of stealing for the game to progress. It is also possible to start feeling repetitive after some time as the gameplay does not allow for much variation to keep it interesting. text_fidelity_a:
Barbie Entomologist Doll and Playset, Blonde, with 20+ Accessories Inspired by National Geographic ... and my girls' too! (Ranging in ages 5-10).

PROs:
--product received is exactly as pictured (we all know online toy purchases can be a gamble)
--the 10 tiny bug pieces included in the kit (which my kids would usually lose within a week) are kept perfrctly in place because they attach practically anywhere upon the included tree, flowers, rock, puddle, and leaves (and are also removeable) so Barbie can also take them to her "lab desk" later to study under the microscope.
--The accessories included were very well-thought out (for example, there is an area on the tree where a butterfly emerges from a cocoon, various pollinators that can "help" the flowers, and Barbie can gather the bugs from the tree and take them back to her "lab desk" to study under the microscope). In other words... this is a VERY "open-ended toy," and as such, would be also be appropriate for learning environments (I homeschool two of my children and also substitute teach preschoolers so open-ended toys that encourage imagination and learning are a MUST)
--Tree and desk are both sturdy enough to stand up without support
--The concept itself is pretty innovative and yet simple: STEM-toy-meets-Barbie is really the best of both worlds and can help encourage a love of science (science IS glamorous and Barbie is gonna prove it haha)
--In my personal experience, it is autism friendly, ADHD friendly, and even adolescent-friendly (I have all 3, and they are having a blast with this toy as we speak)
--a great gift for both kids and classrooms

CONS:
--Yes, this Barbie is high quality (it'll never be mistaken for any Dollar Tree knockoffs) but do keep in mind that this is Entomologist Barbie, NOT Yoga Barbie lol. So tiny fingers might need adult help dressing/accessorizing her.
--Barbie does not stand on her own without support (as is the case for most Barbies).
--no caterpillars included (not complaing because there are 10 bugs in the kit, including the cocoon that turns into a butterfly which was an awesome surprise. But a catepillar in the kit would have been SUPER helpful for helping explain metamorphisis.) All in all, this product is well-thought out, and certainly the coolest Barbie that my "geeky science mom self" has ever come across, so in my book it still deserves 5 stars and honestly more if I could.

If you're on the fence about purchasing this for your budding scientist who happens to love Barbies, go ahead and be the hero and take the plunge.
text_fidelity_b: Barbie Entomologist Doll and Playset, Blonde, with 20+ Accessories Inspired by National Geographic

Dimension - A 3D Fast-Paced Puzzle Game from Kosmos | Up to 4 Players, for Fans of Strategy, Quick-Thinking & Logic | Parents' Choice Silver Honor & Oppenheim Toy Portfolio Platinum Award Winner Though it can at times feel a bit simple, overall Dimension is a fun game that plays quickly and makes for fast, easy to learn family fun.

Packaging and materials: everything in its place, easily held in place, all in good shape, no excessive packaging, easy to open and easy to store back in the box. The balls have a good sense of heft to them, stack easily in their spots, and are well-made. Our son dropped a good number of them the first few times playing and after the first few, our nervousness about the balls breaking or chipping disappeared (though we still wished he’d control their rolls a bit better . . . ) Cards are also well-made, as our the playing boards--heavy stock that come with stick-on feet to hold them slightly off the table surface so the balls don’t move around too easily. All in all, construction is a plus.

Directions: For the most part, directions are quite clear and are pretty minimal. The directions also offer up a few variant forms of the game for making things easier or more challenging, though to be honest, anyone could have come up with those pretty easily and quickly (for instance, upping the number of challenges one has to meet)

Game play.
You each take some point markers to start, and place your 15 spheres--five trios of different colors-- in your game board (again, the balls rest solidly in their holes).

The center of the game board is where you will build patterns with the balls depending on the card challenges. There are seven spaces in the building area, and you can build upward from those spaces, employing up to three layers and up to 11 spheres (7 in your bottom layer, three in the middle layer, and one on top).

You lay out six cards, each one detailing a particular challenge you must meet when you build your patterns. Some examples:
Two specific colors must touch (i.e. somewhere in your pattern, a blue sphere must contact a white sphere
Two specific colors must not touch
You must use a specific number of a particular color
One color must outnumber another (i.e. you must have more green spheres than white spheres)
Two colors must total a specific number (i.e. between blue and white spheres, you must total 4: 1 blue and 3 white, 2 and 2, 1 white and 3 blue)
A particular color cannot be laid atop any of the other colors
A particular color cannot have any of the other colors put on top of it (i.e. your green spheres must be the topmost layer)

once the cards are laid out, you turn over a one-minute timer and try and create a 3-dimensional pattern/pyramid that will meet as many of the challenges as possible.

You get one point for each challenge you meet and lose two points for each one you miss. There is a bonus for meeting all six and/or using all the colors. You also get more points the more spheres you use, though you’ll have to weigh quickly whether adding more spheres to get more points might break a rule and thus lose more than you gain (for instance, adding another blue sphere would get you a point, but if in doing so you broke a rule by having it touch a green sphere, you would lose two points).

As you can see, sometimes the rules may conflict (you might, for instance, get a card that says blue and white must touch and another that says blue and white cannot touch). In those cases, each player decides for him/herself which challenge they choose to ignore.

An entire game is six rounds and most points wins.

It goes very quickly and as you might guess, the speed and difficulty of each round is determined by the combination of cards. Sometimes all three of us were done well before the timer, other times we were all caught with spheres still in our hands trying to figure out where to add or remove a color. And sometimes you’d smoothly and confidently total up your six points for meeting all the challenges and other times as you were oh so cockily adding another challenge to your list you’d suddenly realize, “Doh--how did I end up with a green touching a blue?!”

Mostly the game moves along quickly and the combinations are decently challenging, though we all thought we’d probably move on to doing 8 challenges soon to up the difficulty even more. The only other point I’d make is an electronic timer would be nice as you’re all concentrating so hard on your pyramid that we’d often miss the time running out, or you’d just pluck off a ball to replace with another when someone noticed it was done and you were stuck. We’ve therefore actually taken to using one of our iPhones as a timer to give us a 10-second beep before the full time runs out.

The other nice thing about the game is it is pretty easily modified for playing to younger levels--dump the timer, drop a color, uses only three or four cards. The game can grow with your kids. Certainly even 5-8 year olds can play simpler versions and then grow into more difficult challenges. Fun to play, a bit different, uses some different skills. Recommended.
text_fidelity_b: Dimension - A 3D Fast-Paced Puzzle Game from Kosmos | Up to 4 Players, for Fans of Strategy, Quick-Thinking & Logic | Parents' Choice Silver Honor & Oppenheim Toy Portfolio Platinum Award Winner

I'm a big fan of the hot wheels sets that you can extend with other parts and enjoy in multiple ways. This set, the main launcher and the orange tracks can be used with normal cars and other sets. But obviously the splitter parts can only be used with the one car they give you.

I will say that it is more fun than the last hot wheels set we brought home, which is a closed system in which none of the parts can be used in any other way, and the action of it was lackluster. This set, at least sending the car through the tracks and launching it with the launcher is really cool.

A few of the parts look kind of flimsy, for example there are a few parts that move and function only because of skinny rubber bands that are visible and obvious on the back. I'm not sure I want teeny rubber bands in the same part of the house as a toddler, and i don't see why they couldn't enclose that area or use better parts.

Overall, I feel like this set is going to be really fun for a few days until part of the splitter car is lost, and then I'll harvest what parts we can use with normal cars and move on. It would be a decent choice to perk up a holiday gathering and be fun for a short time, but it packs staying power.

Treasure X King's Gold Treasure Tomb We have had a few other Treasure X sets in the past and my son really enjoyed them, with the sets keeping him busy for hours at a time carving and opening little slime filled packages with interesting toys inside. He has a castle "dollhouse" that he uses a lot of these toys in to create stories.

This treasure tomb was completely different in the sense that we work carving the toys out of chunks of sand this time, rather discovering each element and kind of figuring out everything as a puzzle.

The one criticism I have is that while I would've loved to have set this down and let my son just figure it out, the texture of a few of the things that you were supposed to just pick apart and peel away were not necessarily obvious that they were disposable elements of the toy, so the instruction manual was necessary, and because the instruction manual was not made big and pictorial, I had to sit there while they figured the whole thing out. My six-year-old figured out and understood most of it, but again, the parts that were not obvious that he was allowed to just tear into them really did need my reading the instructions and giving encouragement.

Aside from that minor quibble, this thing kept both my six-year-old and my three and half-year-old busy for a really long time. Hours. I sat them outside on the patio with a big pan to hold any messy elements, and they carved and drove swords into holes and put the keys in and popped everything out and overall had a ridiculously fun time.

The weird textural blue rock like slime in two of the tombs was particularly compelling to my son, who played with this stuff for about 45 minutes. I would've appreciated if the two tombs had had different types of slime or even just different colors, but my son had no such complaint and played for a long time.

While the tomb itself has not continued to hold their interest after about a week of play, some of the parts have been incorporated into frequent play with their castle dollhouse, and so overall even though part of it feels somewhat disposable, the other parts of it feel really fun for incorporating into our normal imaginative play.

This would make a fantastic birthday gift, because it is extremely flashy, tons of fun, lots of excited commentary and wowed children, and then lots of little toys that feel very fun and abundant.

Would I buy a set like this again? Very possibly, for a holiday or other occasion that I really want to feel super special and fancy. If there was a holiday where we were unable to have family and friends visit us or something like that, this set would bridge the gap to make the day feel sparkly and exciting for the kids.
text_fidelity_b: Treasure X King's Gold Treasure Tomb

Pantasy Saint Seiya Building Kit, Sagittarius Aiolos Action Figure Level Building Sets for Adults, Creative Art Collectible Model for Home or Office, Soul of Gold - Saint Cloth Myth EX Building Blocks Pantasy makes amazing building sets, with pieces that usually stay together and super clear instructions. There are some untranslated dialogue boxes here and there, but the diagrams are so clear that I was never confused.

This set of Saint Seiya is something of a mix between a figure and a building set. The base is a traditional building set, and then Saint Seiya is a somewhat poseable figure. The neck, shoulders, knees, ankles, and wings have ball and socket joints for articulation. The elbows have gears that limit movement somewhat. The hips can move forward and backward only. The hands have small ball and socket connectors, but they don’t always hold the positions I set.

I usually really like sets from Pantasy, but this one fell a little short for me in the figure itself. It keeps breaking when I try to put it on the stand, or if I try to pose it too much. This is a set you build and then put on display, somewhere it won’t be bumped. I’ve tried several times to get the feet attached to the base, but end up relying on the clear support on the back of the base, which has a rod to attach to a hole on the figure’s back.

I’ve had the wings fall off, the hands fall off, armor pieces fall off, you name it, it’s fallen off. One of the wings has a loose connection and continually falls off. I have built several sets from Pantasy, none with this problem.

I think the armor is actually fantastic, all metallic gold pieces that match in color. Many of the bigger pieces are wrapped in extra plastic to prevent scratches. The bow and arrow are nestled in foam in a separate box; the packaging is impressive, on par with a UCS set.

There are two face options, and an extra hand if you don’t want to use the bow. There are some great building techniques like SNOT, and as I said, the instructions are very clear. This is an 18+ set, but I think anyone could handle it.
text_fidelity_b: Pantasy Saint Seiya Building Kit, Sagittarius Aiolos Action Figure Level Building Sets for Adults, Creative Art Collectible Model for Home or Office, Soul of Gold - Saint Cloth Myth EX Building Blocks

** IN THE BOX ** Along with the showerhead there is a small roll of teflon thread tape, rubber pipe gasket, in-pipe flow restrictor, and instructions.

** INSTALLATION ** Remove old shower head. Clean pipe threads. Apply 3 turns of pipe thread in a CLOCKWISE direction. Extend shower head extension pipe arm all the way out. If you want flow restriction, insert now, other insert pipe gasket. Attach shower head in a CLOCKWISE direction by hand until tight. Cover the plastic thread cap (nearest the pipe) with a cloth and tighten 1/4 turn with a pliers or pipe wrench using GENTLE pressure. The shower head can now be straightened by gentle turning the adjustment screw (nearest shower head) by hand. It will click. Once you have the general downward direction of the shower head placed, test for leaks. If it leaks at the pipe & shower head connection, gently tighten another 1/4 turn. Once you're ready you can position the shower head, by head, any which way you like . It will click letting you know it's locked.

** USAGE ** Turn water on to your favorite temperature and insert your glorious naked self under the shower head. Look up at the nipples. Yes, there are 90 nipples up there. Very supple nipples that can be squeezed for cleaning. With so many nipples I don't think I'm ever leaving the shower ever again. The 90 nipples provided me an even pressurized rain all over my smelly carcass.

** THOUGHTS ** The TH2.5 works like a charm. Big, even rain all over me. Just what I wanted. Installation was simple provided you have normal shower pipes and are a bit handy with some pliers. The joints articulate well with no movement once set. The joints, once set, should accommodate short and tall humans. I'm 6'1", the wild redhead is 5'7" so this head works amazingly well for both of us. Did I mention there were 90 nipples?

** POINTS OF INTEREST **
- flow is optional and NOT installed
- joints articulate with a solid 'click' and stay in place
- pipe tape and gasket are included
- cover with cloth during final tightening to avoid scratching
- gently squeeze the nipples to clean
- looks like the USS Enterprise from the side... Aye, Aye Captain!
- I just love saying the word 'nipples'
text_fidelity_b: GK Galleria Frozen 2 Birthday Party Supplies for 12 Princesses with 170 Plus Items - Birthday Party Supplies - Frozen Party Decorations - Frozen Plates and Tablecloth - Anna Olaf Elsa

Fisher-Price 3-in-1 Bounce, Stride and Ride Elephant A good toy for toddlers, the Fisher Price 3 in 1 Bounce, Ride and Stride Elephant helps youngsters develop while having fun. The toy lets then bounce, ride, and walk along as they listen to the sounds and enjoy the light up buttons and songs.

This toy is intended for toddlers under the age of 3 and most will take to it right away. Those on the younger side will like bouncing more than anything while those toward the upper end of the recommended age range will like riding and pushing. My youngest child is outside of the recommended age range, but she is lightweight for her age and liked riding the most. It takes a little bit of effort, but with just a small amount of leg power, young children can push themselves along without any assistance.

Kids will love the sounds and lights that are part of this toy. The good news for parents is that you can shut off the sounds- a feature you don’t always get with similar toys. This is nice for adults who get impatient with the constant sounds coming from kids’ toys. In truth, the sound isn’t that loud or that bad with this toy, but it’s nice to know that it can be shut off, if desired.

A toy that encourages activity, keeps kids interested, and helps them develop has all the makings of a keeper and this toy is just that. The price could turn some people away, but it’s not too bad and the fun and other advantages make this toy worth the money.
text_fidelity_b: Fisher-Price 3-in-1 Bounce, Stride and Ride Elephant

text_fidelity_a:
Miko 2: Playful Learning STEM Robot | Programmable + Voice Activated AI Tutor +Autonomous + Educational Games | 30+ Free Apps | Best Birthday Gift for 5 6 7 8 9 Boys and Girls [[VIDEOID:806ce296931b008ec9e325daf5456c6e]] We are owners of a Vector robot by Anki, so we can provide a little perspective. I think you have to at least own one robot in a similar price range to know what is reasonable expectation. If Miko is your first robot, your expectations might be too low or too high. So I think I can give you a balance opinion.

Artificial Intelligence... Vector wins.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Vector is like Pinocchio trying to be a real boy. Miko is a smart device that moves on command. Imagine if Alexa, Siri or Google was given a Robot body in the shape of an egg, that's Miko! If you're looking for a robot that's more independent and feels more real, Vector is what you want. Vector truly feels like a pet with the convenience of never having to feed it or take it for a walk. LOL! When you physically touch or nudge Vector, it reacts. If you tap the floor in front of him, his eyes will look down, if you waive your hand over his head, his head will look up. You can tell it gets excited to see you. It is happy when you stroke it, and gets mad when you lift him in the air for too long. Miko is not like that, nor does Miko move around autonomously like Vector. You have to to initiate "AUTOPILOT" in order for Miko to move around herself. And when she's on autopilot, some default music is playing, basically the theme music you hear in their Miko ads. When she bumps into something, she has a few phrases, one of which is "Not again!" But it all feels programmed, it does not feel like a pet roaming around with independent thinking. It can bump into the same spot over and over. Whereas with Vector, when you put him in a new environment, he will scan the room, and take 360 degree snapshots of his environment so he can roam around more intelligently. When you interrupt him, he'll react, when you pick him up, he gets mad, he wants you to put him down. When you interrupt Miko on Autopilot, nothing happens. You can put your hands in front of her, and she'll move in another direction because of her sensors, but that's about it. If you use the wake word, "Hello Miko," she will respond, but she will no longer be on autopilot, and you'll need to manually start it again. They should at least put an update where you can tell Miko to go on autopilot using voice. It's basically like a Roomba that you set on autopilot. Vector feels like a living thing because you can interrupt him, and interact with him, then when you leave him alone, he goes about his business moving around again. You can tell Vector to come to you, and he will like a real pet. Miko does not come to you like that. She may move forward, but she does not come to your direction. Vector knows where the direction of the command is coming from and he will move towards that direction. You can make a loud banging noise and Vector will react like a nosy human, his head will move as if asking, "What was that noise?" Meanwhile, Miko will stand motionless, there is no reaction to the environment. When Vector's battery is drained, he knows how to find his charging dock and dock himself. Meaning you could be away for awhile, come back and find Vector on his charging dock, but that doesn't mean he hasn't been snooping around. LOL! With Miko, there is no charging dock. She'll let you know she needs more juice, and you'll have to charge her. Lastly, as is, Miko only recognizes one face, whereas Vector can recognize multiple faces and call your correct name. I think Miko actually doesn't even recognize any faces, for that matter. This is how I know... When you introduce yourself and tell her your name, JACK, you become the default profile. Then when you ask Miko "who am I," she'll say JACK correctly. Now if you have someone else introduce herself as JILL, she now becomes the new default. So if Jack comes back and ask, "Who am I?" Miko will say JILL. She basically just calls you by the name of the last person introduced. So currently, there is no intelligent facial recognition like Vector.

Which one has more games and learning apps? Miko wins.
-------------------------------------------------------------------
I guess this would be the bread and butter of Miko. Vector has a tiny interface to show his facial emotions and a few games like black jack, but there's not a lot to do with Vector in terms of apps. He is not app-centric, Miko is app-centric. Both robots have the usual general knowledge AI. You can ask both robots questions like who's the president, what time is it, math, definitions, etc. Basically all the types of general knowledge you would ask Alexa, Siri or Hey Google. But on top of the general knowledge, Miko has a big colorful screen with lots of learning apps. The games will require the child to interact and press buttons to give or to get answers. This is the main advantage Miko has over Vectors. So that's why I say Miko feels like a tablet that moves on command. I guess the plan is for Miko to continue to develop and add to their app store, which is called the TALENT HOUSE. I've seen a coding app that they are asking $30 for. But most apps are free. This would be equivalent to the Skills section of the Alexa app. The more you add, the more things your Miko will do. Again, you want Vector if you want something that feels more life like, something to play with. He has a cube that he likes to play with, so you can ask him to flip his cube, pick up his cube, etc. Like a dog with tricks. Miko has no moving arms, and does not interact physically with you.

Miko has a neat Video calling feature.
--------------------------------------------
Because it has the advantage of the big screen, one neat feature of the Miko is that you can call it from your smartphone, but within the Miko app. I assume this will work from anywhere. It's basically wifi calling with video. So you'll be able to see your kids when they answer, and they'll be able to see you. Can't do that with Vector! You can also move Miko during this video call using directional buttons in the app.

Wake word.. Miko wins.
---------------------------
How is this even a category for competition? LOL! But you see, with Vector, the wake word is "Hey Vector," but you have to wait for him to turn blue, then you have to say "I have a question.." Then wait for Vector to say, "Ready!" Then you can ask your question. This is probably the #1 complaint of Vector. It doesn't feel like a natural conversation like it does with Alexa, Siri or Google. Miko wins here because asking her general questions is just like Alexa. You say, "Hello Miko," when she turns green, you proceed with your question. Not convoluted like Vector. I will say this.. Vector has Alexa built in. So you can actually bypass Vector for general knowledge and just say, "Alexa!" This way, you won't need to say "I have a question." But it's just weird to hear Alexa's voice in Vector's body.

The VOICE.. Vector wins.
----------------------------
Vector sounds like a cute robot. Miko sounds like your very dull and boring Auntie. LOL! There are 4 voices to choose from in Miko's app, one of which is a man's voice, but they don't sound all that much better. For such a cute and colorful device, it's strange to have such dull choices for the voices.

Availability.. Miko wins.
---------------------------
Why am I talking so much about Vector, a robot who's creator company Anki, is out of business? LOL! Well, that's because Digital Dreams Lab has continued on with Vector. They bought the rights, and they were on Kickstarter to provide new life to Vector for a fee, including an escape pod feature that supposedly will allow Vector to be fully functional forever even if Digital Dreams Lab goes out of business. But now, I think Vector cost a little more in the secondary market.

Conclusion:
--------------
There is potential here. Ultimately, I might be comparing apples to oranges. I have no idea about what goes on behind the scenes in AI, programming, coding, etc. The path in development for these two could be so different that asking one to be more like the other could be unreasonable. You can't ask Vector to have more apps and games, right? It wasn't develop with a big screen. Likewise, you probably can't ask Miko to be more like vector since it wasn't built with any arms. I would sum it up as Miko being App-Centric, and Vector is Movement-Centric. If you're interested in something more like a smart device/tablet that could move, get Miko. If you're more interested in the physical interaction with a robot, that's more on the side of a real learning AI, then get Vector.

Reasonable improvements I'd like Miko to make:

-Ability to turn off music in auto pilot.
-Ability to turn on apps, including auto pilot by voice.
-Ability to turn off apps by voice as well. Right now, if Miko is dancing or playing music, you cannot voice her to stop. You have to grab her and push the stop button.

I hope this company sticks around and improves on Miko!

text_fidelity_a:
T.S. Shure Learn to Latch Hook Book & Set This is a great set to introduce kids (as well as adults) to the art of latch hooking. The instruction book is colorful and easy to follow, with clear directions and beautiful graphics. I would give this a five-star review except for two things:

The book gets you and your child excited to start making beautiful projects (including your own customized designs), yet it provides only enough yarn and canvas to make ONE double-sided, child-size pillow. If you want to make bigger and more complicated projects, you have to order more supplies. Because of this, I felt this was more of a "sample" kit, aimed at giving newcomers a "taste" of latch hooking to get you "hooked." For $30, I expected enough material to make at least two projects. Also, what yarn there is of so-so quality - it's rather light and thin, "play yarn" for children, I guess.

Also the packaging felt odd. The book is tied to an empty cardboard box that seems to have no function other than to fill space to make the kit look bigger and more substantial than it is. It's tied so tightly with pipe cleaners that you can't help but tear the back of the book as you try to free it. Another reviewer commented that this may be due to craft stores experiencing a lot of shoplifting - but the book could have been easily secured using double sided tape or light adhesive.

Other than that, this kit will provide hours of enjoyment for adults and kids, especially those (like me) suffering from cabin fever thanks to an interminably long winter. I would definitely buy more as gifts if it were less than the current price.
text_fidelity_b: T.S. Shure Learn to Latch Hook Book & Set

Crayola Triple Tip Markers, Washable Markers, 15 Vivid Colors, 5 Count Soooo, I had high hopes for these markers. I thought my little one would be highly amused by writing in three colors at once (she was mildly amused for a short period of time). I think the issue is that in order to get the even three color lines when writing or stamping or coloring, you have to hold the marker perfectly upright and ensure all three tips are somewhat evenly on the paper. This is not easy for little hands (my little one is almost 3). I myself had to concentrate to create the images I posted. It's much easier to end up with 2 of the colors in a line or even one depending on how you hold the marker.

The colors individually are nice, but sometimes when they cross over, they create kind of ugly mixes and combinations. Again, this depends on how steadily you hold the marker and what colors you have on top or bottom (as shown by the squiggles under my first picture).

All in all, I would call this an interesting novelty - for slightly older kids. I'm guessing my little one might make some stamps and then these will go in with the rest of the markers. If she was doing more freeform drawing - it might be more amusing.
text_fidelity_b: Crayola Triple Tip Markers, Washable Markers, 15 Vivid Colors, 5 Count

PopSockets Fidget Train with Expanding PopSockets , Premium Fidget Toy, ASMR, Toys for Adults and Kids I am a terrible fidget and I am always on the lookout for toys and gizmos that will keep me focused so I can sit still and not distract everyone around me. I selected this thinking it would be similar to those blister-type pop toys. It's not, but it's still an effective toy for stress relief and focus. It's possibly a little too noisy for a meeting, though.

At a glance this thing looks like the sections might come apart. They do not. Instead, this is an accordion-style fidget toy that you pull and push on the ends to make it expand and contract. It can be bent, twisted slightly, partially expanded and completely expanded. The colors are soothing and the tactile feel is nice.

When expanding the toy the sections are not silent. They're not loud, but they have a noticeable popping sound that's lost in the background in a normal environment but draws attention to itself in a more quiet area like a meeting room. It can be expanded more quietly with a little thought. If in an area where making a small amount of noise is acceptable, the sound is satisfying.

As I write this, this toy is close to $30 which seems high. This is really my only reservation with it.

I like this toy and will get some good use out of it. I usually mess with it when I am sitting at my desk and I want to sit still. It has a satisfying sound when popped, it's easy to work, and it looks pretty. It's a little on the expensive side, though.

LEGO Star Wars Millennium Falcon Microfighter 75193 Building Kit (92 Pieces) If you have a 6 year old who is into Star Wars and who also loves Legos (or maybe you would like to get them into Legos and/or Star Wars), then this is a great Lego kit to do just that. I bought this and the one with the bad guy for my son's Easter Basket. Being a "connoisseur" of Star Wars and Legos, my son lost his mind when he saw what the Easter Bunny brought.

The Lego Microfighters are mini vehicles you build, which you can use to either expand your Lego-verse or play with separately. These come with instructions on how to build the microfighter. They are simple to put together, but I would not advise this for a child younger than 6 unless you know your 4 or 5 year old is really good at Lego instructions (which are in picture form). These are not ideal for children who are still primarily freebuilders or just learning about Legos. You should get the creative set for that. However, if your child loves to freebuild, but can also follow instructions this is a great gift! My son built all of the microfighters as designed, played with them for a bit, and then rearranged them to his freebuilding heart's desire. I cut the instructions apart and rearrange them in plastic sleeves so that if he wants to build according to the instructions they are neat and organized. Also do not let the "Micro" fool you, they are regular sized Legos, they will work with other Legos, it's just that they are really small scaled models. Also, the Lego people (Chewbacca) that come the sets are regular sized Lego people. So, their body parts can be mixed and matched with others you have in your collection.

One Caveat: For some odd reason, these sets as well as some of the smaller Lego City sets always have their boxes just crushed and in horrible shape. So, if you are looking for these are gift, I usually purchase from a store like Target, Walmart, or the Lego store itself to pick out the very best box. I'm not sure why Lego does this. I used to blame Target, but then I realized this was a Lego issue and not a store issue.
text_fidelity_b: LEGO Star Wars Millennium Falcon Microfighter 75193 Building Kit (92 Pieces)

Diamond Painting Stickers Kits for Kids, Paint by Numbers Diamonds for Adult Beginners,DIY 5D Diamond Art Mosaic Stickers I have the “28PCS POKEMON” option in this pack of diamond painting stickers from BLYNN. This option is really a multipack of different themes: Pokemon (12 stickers), Star Wars (8 stickers), and Princesses (8 stickers).

This is a great way to try diamond painting since the images are small. They vary in size, but are roughly 3 inches by 3 inches. An image this size takes about 30 minutes for a beginner. When you are finished putting the diamond drills on the image, you can peel off the back and it’s a sticker.

The pack includes two toolkits, so you can have two kids working on their chosen sticker at the same time. The diamond paintings can be cut apart -- I recommend an adult do this part, since the edges are close together -- and then worked on separately. That way you don’t have to remove the protective plastic from the whole sheet.

The pack also includes the drills for every sticker. Some of the colors are really off. Snorlax should be dark teal, but the drills are dark green. Eevee should be brown, but the drills are yellow-orange. The drills come in tear-open plastic baggies; I recommend having some small resealable baggies or containers ready if you aren’t going to do all of the stickers at once, since they often share colors (like yellow-orange for Eevee and Charmander).

And while I am still can't decide if that is a good thing or not, I do think that this version will appeal to most. While I can usually "trick" my 10 and 13 year old sons to play Classic Uno, I wondered would this version of the game appeal to them more because it has a computerized component. After all, the robot is cute with it's little voice, and the cards fit nicely in a holder on it's head. Especially because today's generation plays XBox, Nintendo, PSP, and the WII. I hoped that they would enjoy it especially on family night.

Surprisingly, this version was extremely interactive, entertaining and tons of fun....throwing out names and house rules, which provided a new twist to an already enjoyable game. The "new" additions to the Classic include: the ability to record the names of the players; the ability to add creative house rules where the last person to complete the task draws two cards; and the ability to add surprise commands. In other words, you can make this game as funny as you want.And while my kids initially thought it was lame, they have asked to play it several times creating silly rules and cute nicknames. I definitely think this game will appeal to some.
text_fidelity_b: Mattel Games UNO: Roboto Game

text_fidelity_a:
Bop It XT Finding a children's toy that can actually entertain....especially during a time (in our country) where kids spend most of there time on the IPod Touch, Xbox, WII, PSP, computers etc. is difficult. We live in a society of computer generated video games, computer enhanced movies, 3D, 4D, special effects, etc, and I find myself asking my kids -what happened to Connect 4, Twister, Simon, UNO, Clue, Life, Scrabble, PAC Man and Monopoly? Basically my childhood was filled with memories of playing these kinds of games, meaning those that essentially force you to interact with people. Under this belief, seeing the "Bop It " I thought maybe ...just maybe my kids (10 & 13) would enjoy playing this on family night. Believe it or not, while it is not animated and gloomy, it gave us hours of pure, clean fun. We battled each other. We laughed and teased. While the game kind of reminded me of Simon, it was surprisingly a bit more complicated. For Simon you just have to remember the color sequences, while the Bop challenges you to complete several tasks.....to pull, twist, flick, roll... quickly or you're out. The minute you miss, you have to start again. There is also a commentator giving the score, and teasing the player. My 13-year-old thought that this would be fun game to take on road trips (to play between all of his other electronics), while my 10-year-old is more determined than ever to beat his present score. Both found "Bop It" to be an easy to understand/fun game that promotes coordination and interacting with others. I highly recommend it.

It's light-weight and easy to carry.
It's stylish. Looks a little Jazzy...each task is a different color and shape.
It would definitely teach kids to listen. Following directions is a crucial element for playing the game.
text_fidelity_b: Bop It XT

Glitter Girls - Convertible Car for 14-inch Dolls - Toys, Clothes & Accessories for Girls 3-Year-Old & Up, Blue, Orange, Pink This convertible car for 14 inch dolls is completely awesome. We have a number of glitter girls dolls and two of them can fit into this convertible with ease, along with one of the glitter girls puppies sitting on a lap.

My kids saw this in a Christmas catalog and were completely enchanted with it, asking for it over and over again. It's about as big as you would expect given that the glitter girls both have to fit in there, and it has a dashboard that opens, a little side container that opens in between the two seats, two cupholders, and the trunk.

We have the glitter girls sweetshop and the accessories sweetshop that has some delightful cups of confectionery beverage, and I was delighted to find that these sweetshop beverages fit into the cupholders perfectly. (They also fit into the girls hands). The dashboard has very little room to put things in when it's open, and the angle is such that things really don't stay put very well at the dashboard is open, so I would've liked a little bit better design on that, because my kids had to work hard to find something they wanted to bring along that was small enough to fit. Same thing with the little container in between the two seats, if that could have been just a little bit wider, it would get used even more.

The trunk is also a little small and again the shape of the interior of it makes it harder for things to fit in, because it is just a rectangular box opening that is kind of slick, so when you put things in the kind of want to slide out. There is enough room in the car to where they could have made the trunk much more substantial, and it would've made this an even cooler car.

That said, these are just quibbles and the real proof of whether a toy is any good is in the pudding. My kids love it, and they've been playing with it nonstop and vrooming the girls around on all kinds of adventures since the car arrived. I've been delighted to see the amount of imaginative play that has taken place with the addition of a car, to where the girls can leave the bedroom and go on all kinds of fun adventures.

The car seems well-made and is very sturdy, the doors open, and if you need to put the windshield down for storage, it does fold down. Overall this is a great toy if you have 14 inch dolls who need some adventure in their lives.

I have flown many of these and my son wanted to try one to get started with. He picked it up really quickly and together we were able to fly it around the house indoors without hitting anything. The camera is gimmicky at best, but for the price I'd say get it for the drone flight fun and forget the camera.
UNTIL... within 2 days of owning it, something seemed to go wrong with the height sensor (barometer?), and it not only wouldn't hold the correct height like it did the day before, but suddenly it shot straight UP. No pressing down on the joystick seems to change anything. Its as if the unit felt like it was falling and needed to compensate by flying more aggressively upwards. It hit the ceiling, and we promptly hit the kill switch. I took a look at it, pulled off the propellers to look, and tried again. Same thing - it shot straight UP. Hit the ceiling. I tried cleaning any hair/debris from the blades and again- straight up until it hit. But this time, it started making a funny noise. Upon closer inspection I found one of the pins that the propeller sits on has been bent. I don't know if this was caused by it going straight up or if it caused it, but the drone has been grounded for now. You can see in the attached video how when that pin is spun, it tilts forward and back, rather that the other pins which spin in place.
It is possibly that I just got a dud and others would love this, I wouldn't mind trying it again and seeing if I have a different outcome. It did work really well for the first 2 days, and I really like that it not only has a replaceable battery but comes with 2 additional batteries as well! Flight times are usually small on these things so having many extra batteries ready to go is useful. If it hadn't gone nuts and shot upwards everytime, I'd give this thing 5 stars. I'm going to see what I can about sourcing a replacement or additional unit and come back to update this review if it turns out I had a lemon.

Even with the lowest magnification lens attached The Housemate and I were able to see Saturn and discern the gap between the planet and its rings. With a higher magnification, things became much clearer, and even more exciting. The first clear image of the moon took my breath away.

The drawbacks? It's very hard to use standing up. I realize it's made for children, but I think a taller tripod might have been a plus here. Even sitting we had to hunch down to see anything at a 45 degree angle or above. Also, the viewfinder did not help at all. I found all the objects we wanted to see by sighting along the barrel of the telescope itself. Now possibly I attached the viewfinder the wrong way, though there really only seems to be one way to do it. Either way, we saw what we intended to see which made the exercise worthwhile.

Why a telescope? Aren't you and your children worth it? Don't you want to learn more about even our part of the universe? This is an amazing gift for the children in your life, or even for yourself. It's lightweight and easy to transport and with the help of something like Google Sky, you can figure out what it is you're looking at with ease. It's a step on the road to becoming better educated in Astronomy, and it should spark a sense of wonder anyone who looks up and longs to know more.

It’s a decent set up it lacks some fit and finish that would make it better.

Included in the set is the Mancala board and a plastic bag with multiple colored stones. There is also a concise rulebook on how to play one variant of the game - overall, a decent starter set.

There are several things about this set that make it less than ideal. The most serious problem is the board which has multiple issues. First, it feels unfinished with several very rough spots that are actually visibly rough. This doesn’t make the game unplayable but it does take away. My board is not routed properly and it looks like the design was routed by hand and wasn’t cleaned up properly with wood shavings wedged in the grooves. The reservoirs are shallow and it is easy to spill the stones while playing.

The stones are another matter. There are enough stones to play. However, there are no extras at all and if one or more are lost the game cannot be played correctly without replacements. And, there’s no container beyond a cheap plastic zipper bag for the stones; a cup with a snap-on lid, or a cloth pouch, would be so much better.

This is a playable and functional set, lacking in finishing touches that differentiate it from a good one.

text_fidelity_a: Lovinouse 1500 Pieces Jigsaw Puzzle Board with 2 Sorting Tray, Portable Puzzles Storage Case Saver, Non-Slip Surface I have been using a large, wooden puzzle board with trays for the pieces. When I saw this, I was intrigued with the ability to tightly close it up without destroying the work in progress. The wooden one will keep the puzzle safe, but you have to find a large place to set it when you're not working on it. So I started a 500 piece puzzle on this board. It's got a fuzzy surface which makes it non-slip. That is good at times, but there are times when I will work on a section of a puzzle and slide it to it's destination. That's difficult to do with this one. Instead of puzzle trays, it has flat fuzzy pieces that you can put the pieces on and move around as needed. With my 500 piece puzzle, I couldn't get all of the pieces spread out flat on the combined boards. I had to have some stacked on top of one another. After I had completed the border, I decided to stop for the evening. I put the puzzle boards on top of the main puzzle area where my work was. Then I closed everything up and made sure the velcro pieces were secure. Then I tilted the whole unit at a 90 degree angle. I heard pieces moving around. My heart sank. The border is always a lot of work! I opened it back up and while the pieces had moved around, it was only the pieces that hadn't been assembled yet. The work area with my completed border was still in tact. I think I will feel better leaving this on a flat surface, such as a table when it's not in use. It does keep the cats from sitting on my work and that's a plus. I always had to cover my work with a towel or something with the wooden tray. This is also weighs less than the wooden one which makes it easier to move. Overall, I am pleased with this puzzle storage piece.

Mainstreet Classics 18-Inch Backgammon Board Game Set The nicest part of this Main Street Classic Backgammon Set is the white topstitching on the black leatherette case which gives it a high quality look. Unfortunately, the set I received has a couple of creases in the fabric interior lining which continually attract my eyes and I always want to play the side without the creases. Because I'm a good sport, I always ask that my opponent select sides and I therefore always wind up with the creases to call my own. The set is not heavy and I appreciate the absence of a weighty and cumbersome handle, but if a handle is important to you for carrying, then this is not the set for you. The "stones" or round pieces have a nice weight to them and I also like the look and feel of all five dice. The cups are just fine in appearance and heft as long as you don't look at the workmanship closely, especially on the bottom where I fear the glue will not be effective for too long. The "manual" is extremely difficult to read because the imprint is faint and some of the words/diagrams are not legible, but as a plus, it does include a paragraph on the history of the game. With a better manual, I think I would have been more impressed with this set, but the included sheet of paper gives a very cheap and careless impression of the manufacturer. One can find resources for the game rules online or in game books and these are easier to read, so I'd suggest that if Main Street is not interested in providing worthwhile instructions, they'd be better off leaving this weak attempt out of the set.

All in all, the workmanship in stitching is excellent but the glue is lacking in the construction of the game I received. I enjoy playing the game, like the look of it, appreciate that it's far superior to the heavy pleather set I had many years ago, but I'm not excited about the retail cost.
text_fidelity_b: Mainstreet Classics 18-Inch Backgammon Board Game Set

Her 7 year old friend was confused until I showed her how to work through the patterns in the book. The friend's 9 year old brother thought it was cool. In my mind it's a preliminary to engines -- combining parts and making them move. My 3 year old learned the word axle. This toy gets pulled out every time we have older kids over to visit. Everyone gets interested in it. It's true that the handle and the animals are hard to keep stuck on the top. The pegs have to be fully pushed into the board or they stick up above the wheel. If the peg sticks up, the toppers won't stay on top. (Manufacturing tolerances just aren't what they used to be!)

I think there is a type of child that this toy will appeal to. My girl likes to do pattern matching and puzzles. This toy is a natural for that. It's easy to see where a child who is (really athletic, really into dramatic play, really into ______) wouldn't get that much out of it. But it's a great toy for the budding engineers out there.

Eighty Eight Miracles Mystical Gold Foil and Black Tarot Cards with Guide Book for Beginner Tarot Readers; Large Tarot Deck Extensive Guidebook Symbolic Meanings of Past History and Future Destiny The cards are a high quality material that seem to be a rigid poly, but I'm not going to do a tear test. The guilding is quite beautiful and it's actually one of my favorite shades of gold hot-foil (there are dozens, lol). The edges are completely foiled and look beautiful when stacked. The back of the cards use a mix of the gold foil and taupe ink. The face of the cards are not foiled at all, but the taupe shade is both attractive and visible in low white, red, green, blue, and even black light. On that note, the manufacturers were smart enough to use UV reactive paper in the guide, so reading it while working should be easy.
This is my first deck and I'm looking forward to having lots of fun with it. Considering the size, they were surprisingly easy to shuffle like playing cards. For what it's worth, my first (ever) self reading was excessively accurate.
The artwork is top-tier, clean, and "finished" looking. Idk if it matters, but the images don't match up perfectly with the descriptions in the guide book. Aside from this, the guidebook is well written and makes it easy to understand (or at least grasp) the meanings and concepts of the cards. There's also a short guide showing several basic card layouts for both self readings and working with others.
I would definitely recommend these as either a personal or gift set. I think it would be attractive enough for professional work, but that would depend on the look you're after (they don't use ANY colors in the artwork besides the taupe ink).
text_fidelity_b: Eighty Eight Miracles Mystical Gold Foil and Black Tarot Cards with Guide Book for Beginner Tarot Readers; Large Tarot Deck Extensive Guidebook Symbolic Meanings of Past History and Future Destiny

text_fidelity_a:
Star Realms: Deckbuilding Game What can I say? This has quickly become my favorite card/board game for several reasons.

1. It's quick. Many games can take hours to play. We play best 2/3, and it usually takes about an hour. Or: about 20 minutes per game.

2. It's variable. What flops on the first turn can change the whole game, because each player has to react to it. Each player is, of course, also reacting to the other player. This translates into a number of different strategies, so each time you play it, it ends up being 'new' in some way, even if you're playing with the same person. This variability makes it more fun because you can never just 'phone it in'.

3. It's easy to learn. There aren't too many rules, so you can teach it to a new player in a few minutes. Of course, they usually have to play several games before they start winning, but that's just a matter of learning the different strategies involved.

Conclusion: HIGHLY recommended.
text_fidelity_b: Star Realms: Deckbuilding Game

text_fidelity_a: Foxnovo Universal Tall Landing Gear Skid for DJI F450 F550 Sk480 Multirotor Quadcopter These legs are the perfect upgrade for the Syma X8C (white) if you're going to be using a different camera. The stock legs are just too short to allow you to mount any kind of adjustable camera rigging and GoPro type camera. You will need to do some drilling in these legs (and shave off the mounting alignment flange of the quad) to make them fit. But, it's worth it. This pic is of the same legs (black) on my Syma X8G (same body as the C, just a different color) and these legs on my Syma X8C. These legs give you the spread and stability you need, as well as the height. They're rigid, strong and don't weigh much more than the stock legs. I've seen some negative reviews regarding 'flimsiness'. I think that anyone should keep in mind the original configuration calls for bracing between the legs, in such a way that actually provides more structural integrity to each leg. Therefore, no bracing means less rigidity, the greater the chances of breakage. Having said that, I've been flying my Syma X8 quads with these for a while now. One of which was totaled. Seriously, the quad dropped like a rock from about 150 feet, crashing through trees and broke HARD. I had to do a total rebuild with new body, motor mounts, gears, etc.The only parts re-used were the control board and motors and the LEGS, which DID NOT BREAK!
text_fidelity_b: Foxnovo Universal Tall Landing Gear Skid for DJI F450 F550 Sk480 Multirotor Quadcopter

Inside the box is a printed city street layout. The paper is very thin, so this won’t last long unless it’s glued to some sort of heavier backing. However the street layout fits the assembled tow truck, and is a nice detail.

Note that this is a LEGO duplo model, intended for very young children. The pieces are much larger than standard LEGO pieces. They are compatible with other duplo building sets, but NOT with standard LEGO elements.
